o: Each query asks for max nums1[j]+nums2[j] subject to nums1[j] ≥ x and nums2[j] ≥ y — a 2-D dominance-maximum problem with n, q up to 1e5, so per-query scanning (O(n·q)) is too slow and we need offline processing. Sort points by nums1 descending and queries by x descending; then when answering a query, all not-yet-inserted points satisfy the nums1 constraint, reducing the problem to: among inserted points, maximize sum subject to nums2 ≥ y. Maintain a monotonic stack keyed by nums2 in decreasing order, storing alongside each nums2 the best sum achievable with any nums2 at least that large. Then each query is a single binary search.
k: Process points and queries together in decreasing order of the nums1/x coordinate to eliminate one dimension offline.
A point (b, s) is useless if another stacked point has nums2 ≥ b and sum ≥ s; the stack therefore has strictly decreasing nums2 and strictly increasing best-sums.
Answer a query by binary-searching the smallest stacked nums2 ≥ y; its stored best-sum is the answer.

a.i: For each query, iterate over all indices and take the maximum sum among those satisfying both constraints. Simple and correct; fine only for tiny inputs.
s: For each query (x, y), scan all j.
Keep max of nums1[j]+nums2[j] where nums1[j]>=x and nums2[j]>=y.

a.n: Approach 2: Offline Sorting + Monotonic Stack + Binary Search
a.i: Sort indices by nums1 descending and queries by x descending. Insert points one by one; before inserting point (b, a+b), pop stack entries with nums2 ≤ b (they are dominated: smaller nums2 and no better sum), track the max popped sum, and push (b, max(that, a+b)). The stack's nums2 values decrease and best-sums increase, so a query with threshold y is answered by binary search for the first entry with nums2 ≥ y.
s: Create point list (nums1[j], nums2[j]) sorted by nums1 descending; sort queries by x descending with original indices.
Pointer p walks points; while nums1[p] >= x, insert point into the stack with domination popping.
For the query, binary search the stack for the smallest nums2 >= y; record its best-sum (or -1).
Restore original query order and return.
a.t: O((n + q) log(n + q)) — sorting dominates; each point enters/leaves the stack once
a.sp: O(n + q) — stack, sorted orders, output

w: Always present the offline-sorting approach; brute force is only a correctness baseline. Common pitfalls: forgetting to carry the maximum popped sum into the newly pushed entry (the pushed best-sum must dominate everything popped), and mishandling ties (pop on <=, not <). Follow-ups: online version (use a segment tree over compressed nums2 with max-sum, or a 2D structure like a BIT of monotonic stacks).
